metadata.title: Pink Floyd: sound, image and time
metadata.subtitle: A source-linked chronology of the music, people, performances and visual experiments
metadata.editorial_scope: A comprehensive selection of major milestones, not an exhaustive gigography, sessionography or solo discography.
metadata.date_policy: Dates preserve the precision supported by the cited sources. Studio album cards normally use the UK release date; differing US dates are explicitly noted. Month/year values are not shorthand for the first day.
metadata.album_count_policy: The standard fifteen-album sequence includes Ummagumma, a hybrid live/studio double album, once. Live albums, compilations, anniversary editions and solo releases are not counted as additional studio albums.
metadata.source_policy: Primary sources: official band chronology, official album pages, dated artist/label announcements, participant production notes and the host museum. Retrospective metadata conflicts are documented and more specific contemporary announcements take priority.
metadata.copyright_note: All event summaries are original paraphrases. No song lyrics or copied review passages are included. Media licensing and embed permissions are handled separately from this factual chronology.

events.title: Pink Floyd takes shape
events.summary: London brings Syd Barrett, Roger Waters, Richard Wright and Nick Mason into the group that becomes Pink Floyd. Barrett supplies a name drawn from blues musicians Pink Anderson and Floyd Council. Cambridge friendships and the London student music scene form the foundations of a band soon moving beyond its rhythm-and-blues beginnings.
notes: Formation is a process, not a documented single-day event; this entry deliberately uses year precision.

source_usage.scope: title, date and summary; precision notes are editorial, with the departure month supplied by timeline-1985

events.title: A home in the London underground
events.summary: Pink Floyd develops its improvisational identity amid London’s underground scene, playing the Marquee’s Spontaneous Underground, London Free School events and the emerging UFO club. Extended music and projected light become parts of one experience. These small rooms establish an approach to performance that later expands into much larger spaces.
notes: The year groups several related venues and engagements, rather than assigning one opening-night date.

source_usage.scope: title, date and summary; precision notes are editorial, with the departure month supplied by timeline-1985

events.title: Arnold Layne reaches the record shops
events.summary: The UK release of Arnold Layne introduces Syd Barrett’s songwriting to listeners. Recorded at Sound Techniques, it takes Pink Floyd beyond its underground following. The band balances concise pop records with the extended improvisations that distinguish its concerts and identity.
notes: Date is the UK single release.

events.title: Games for May puts sound in motion
events.summary: At London’s Queen Elizabeth Hall, Games for May places Pink Floyd in a concert-hall setting with a deliberately theatrical presentation. The Azimuth Co-ordinator allows sound to move around the room. The show makes spatial audio and the audience’s physical surroundings central parts of the band’s developing visual and musical language.
notes: This describes a documented early surround-sound experiment; it does not claim the invention of surround sound.

source_usage.scope: title, date and summary; note is an original editorial qualification

events.title: See Emily Play becomes a UK hit
events.summary: See Emily Play is released and reaches number six on the UK singles chart. Barrett’s compact, imaginative pop songwriting brings the group to a wider audience, including television. The single offers another entrance into a band whose stage performances can already stretch far beyond the three-minute format.
notes: Date is the UK single release, not the date of its chart peak.

events.title: The Piper at the Gates of Dawn
events.summary: Pink Floyd’s debut combines Barrett’s concise, eccentric songs with the exploratory spirit of the band’s live improvisations. Recorded with producer Norman Smith, it is the only album to feature Barrett throughout. Its title comes from The Wind in the Willows, placing a literary pastoral image beside the group’s electric experimentation.
notes: UK release: 4 August 1967. The official chronology dates the differently configured US edition to 21 October 1967.

events.title: Five musicians, then a new quartet
events.summary: David Gilmour joins Pink Floyd, briefly creating a five-piece band with Barrett, Waters, Wright and Mason. The official chronology records the five-piece debut at Aston University on 12 January and a Southampton performance without Barrett on 26 January. The transition changes both the stage lineup and the band’s songwriting balance.
notes: This card covers the January performing transition. Barrett’s formal separation and management changes unfolded over the following months; it is not a claim that he formally left on 26 January.

events.title: A Saucerful of Secrets
events.summary: The second album captures the change from Barrett’s band to the Gilmour, Waters, Wright and Mason quartet. Recordings from both periods sit together, including Barrett’s Jugband Blues. The title piece develops a larger structural approach, while Hipgnosis begins the album-cover relationship that becomes inseparable from Pink Floyd’s visual identity.
notes: Date is the UK release. Barrett appears on three tracks according to the official album guide.

events.title: The Man and The Journey
events.summary: At the Royal Festival Hall, Pink Floyd presents two extended concert suites, The Man and The Journey. Parts of the music later appear as individual pieces including Grantchester Meadows and Biding My Time. The programme shows the band thinking beyond a succession of songs toward a concert with a larger dramatic progression.
notes: The date is the Royal Festival Hall presentation recorded in the official chronology.

events.title: More
events.summary: The soundtrack for Barbet Schroeder’s film More sends Pink Floyd into music built around dramatic scenes and settings. Short songs and instrumental passages coexist, with the film sometimes placing the music inside the action through radios or other playback devices. Several pieces also find an independent life in the band’s concerts.
notes: The year-by-year official chronology gives 13 June 1969 for the UK album release. The general biography’s July date is not used.

events.title: Live music for the moon landing
events.summary: Pink Floyd supplies live music for the BBC’s television coverage surrounding the first Moon landing. The performance known as Moonhead connects the band’s atmospheric improvisation to an event unfolding in real time. It is a distinctive meeting of experimental rock, broadcasting and the imagery of the space age.
notes: The official chronology dates the appearance to 20 July; the BBC coverage extended across the night.

events.title: Ummagumma
events.summary: Ummagumma divides a double album between live performances and separate studio contributions from each of the four musicians. Concert pieces show the group’s collective power, while the studio record exposes contrasting individual interests. Its hybrid format makes it an unusual entry in the standard sequence of fifteen Pink Floyd studio albums.
notes: The official chronology dates the UK release to 7 November and the US release to 8 November 1969. This is a live/studio hybrid, counted once in the standard fifteen-album sequence.

events.title: Atom Heart Mother
events.summary: A side-long title work brings brass and choir into Pink Floyd’s music, with Ron Geesin helping shape the expanded arrangement. The second side returns to smaller songs and the domestic sounds of Alan’s Psychedelic Breakfast. The record becomes the band’s first UK number-one album, enlarging both its scale and audience.
notes: UK release: 2 October 1970. Official chronology gives 10 October for the US release.

events.title: Performing inside an empty amphitheatre
events.summary: Filming begins in the ancient amphitheatre at Pompeii under director Adrian Maben. Pink Floyd performs without a conventional concert audience, letting the musicians, equipment and surrounding ruins carry the images. The encounter between a contemporary electric band and an ancient site becomes one of its defining audiovisual documents.
notes: Four days of location filming began on 4 October 1971; additional filming took place later in Paris. The film’s premiere belongs to 1972.

events.title: Meddle
events.summary: Meddle brings contrasting shorter pieces together with Echoes, which occupies the whole second side. The extended work grows from experiments and fragments developed by the musicians, becoming a demonstration of sustained collective composition. One of These Days gives the album another lasting live centrepiece, built around a very different kind of momentum.
notes: Date is the UK release. The official chronology dates the US release to 30 October 1971, before the British issue.

events.title: Dark Side is tested in front of audiences
events.summary: At Brighton Dome, Pink Floyd attempts an early performance of the suite that will become The Dark Side of the Moon. Equipment trouble interrupts the presentation. The developing work continues through subsequent concerts, giving the musicians a public workshop for material that will change before the finished studio album arrives.
notes: This was an early work in progress, not playback of the finished 1973 album.

events.title: Obscured by Clouds
events.summary: A second collaboration with Barbet Schroeder produces music for La Vallée. Recorded near Paris, Obscured by Clouds favours compact songs and instrumental pieces while Dark Side is still developing onstage and in the studio. The parallel projects show the band moving between film deadlines, concise writing and a larger conceptual work.
notes: UK release: 2 June 1972. Official chronology gives 17 June for the US release.

events.title: Live at Pompeii reaches the screen
events.summary: Live at Pompeii premieres at the Edinburgh International Film Festival. Adrian Maben’s film transforms performances recorded the previous year into a cinema experience, making the empty amphitheatre part of the drama. Its release date is separate from the recording dates, a distinction that later restorations make especially useful to preserve.
notes: Premiere date follows the official chronology. Later versions of the film contain additional material.

events.title: The Dark Side of the Moon
events.summary: After a year of live development, The Dark Side of the Moon links songs, voices and sound effects around everyday pressures: time, work, money and mortality. Engineer Alan Parsons and vocalist Clare Torry are among its important collaborators. The prism sleeve, credited to Hipgnosis and George Hardie, gives the studio experience an equally concentrated visual identity.
notes: Month precision is intentional. The official album guide says March 1973; specific release days differ between retrospective accounts and markets.

events.title: An album imagined from household sounds
events.summary: Pink Floyd explores a project known as Household Objects, using everyday items as musical sources. The sessions with Alan Parsons test how far the band might push the studio after Dark Side. The proposed album does not emerge as planned, but the experiment belongs to the same history of treating sound itself as composition.
notes: The chronology gives 1 October as a session date; this broader project card uses month precision.

events.title: The circular screen enters the show
events.summary: The French tour introduces Pink Floyd’s circular projection screen, giving films and images a strong architectural place above the musicians. New material also appears onstage, including Shine On You Crazy Diamond and Raving and Drooling. During the year, touring becomes a workshop for music that will feed more than one future album.
notes: The official chronology dates the start of this French tour to 18 June 1974. The screen and developing songs are grouped as a tour milestone.

events.title: Wish You Were Here
events.summary: Wish You Were Here explores absence and the pressures of the music business, with the Barrett tribute Shine On You Crazy Diamond framing the record. The band builds an emotional world around spacious playing and uneasy relationships. Hipgnosis extends those ideas into the artwork, making absence a visual theme as well as a musical one.
notes: UK release: 12 September 1975; the official chronology gives 13 September for the US. No precise date is assigned here to Barrett’s unannounced studio visit.

events.title: A pig above Battersea
events.summary: The Animals cover shoot places an inflatable pig above Battersea Power Station. Across several days, weather, photographic choices and an escaped balloon complicate the plan. The resulting cover combines images from different moments, showing how a carefully constructed photograph can become as memorable as the music it is designed to introduce.
notes: Shoot ran 2–4 December 1976. The official account places the escape on the second day and describes a composite final image.

events.title: Animals
events.summary: Animals turns long-form music toward a sharp social allegory influenced by George Orwell’s Animal Farm. Earlier live pieces are transformed into Dogs and Sheep, joined by Pigs (Three Different Ones) and the shorter Pigs on the Wing. The record gives the band’s mid-seventies experiments a more confrontational political focus.
notes: UK release: 21 January 1977. Official chronology gives 12 February for the US release.

events.title: The stadium and the imagined wall
events.summary: The In the Flesh tour ends in Montreal amid a strained relationship between performer and audience. Waters’ response to the experience helps generate the idea of a barrier separating a rock band from its listeners. The Wall develops from that image into a much broader story about isolation and the forces that create it.
notes: This links a documented concert to Waters’ subsequent concept; it does not reduce the entire album to a single incident.

events.summary: Waters begins demoing ideas for The Wall and The Pros and Cons of Hitch Hiking at Britannia Row. The projects eventually take different paths, as a Pink Floyd album and a Waters solo album. Gilmour and Wright also issue solo records in 1978, making the musicians’ individual creative interests increasingly visible.

events.summary: Another Brick in the Wall, Part 2 becomes Pink Floyd’s first UK single release since 1968. Its arrival shortly before The Wall brings one part of a sprawling concept album into the pop charts. The record reaches number one in Britain, making the band highly visible in a format it had largely set aside.

events.title: The Wall
events.summary: The Wall follows the fictional rock star Pink through a story of injury, withdrawal and confrontation. Waters’ concept becomes a double album produced with David Gilmour and Bob Ezrin, while Gerald Scarfe supplies its distinctive visual vocabulary. The work is designed to expand beyond records into an unusually integrated stage production and film.
notes: UK release: 30 November 1979. The official chronology gives 8 December for the US release.

events.title: The Wall becomes a physical concert
events.summary: The first Wall concerts open in Los Angeles. A structure assembled during the performance turns the album’s central metaphor into a visible barrier between musicians and audience. Music, projection and stage action operate together, bringing Pink Floyd’s long interest in concert environments to an especially literal and elaborate form.
notes: This is the opening of the original Pink Floyd production; subsequent Waters productions are separate events.

events.title: The Wall premieres at Cannes
events.summary: Alan Parker’s film of The Wall premieres at Cannes, with a screenplay by Roger Waters and Bob Geldof in the central role. Cinema gives the story another life after the album and concerts. The project carries Pink Floyd’s music and visual world across three distinct forms, each with its own way of presenting the narrative.

events.title: The Final Cut
events.summary: The Final Cut develops from proposed Wall-related material into an album shaped by the Falklands War, remembrance and contemporary politics. Richard Wright is absent from the recording lineup. It is the last Pink Floyd album with Roger Waters, whose anti-war writing and tribute to his father give the record its unusually personal focus.
notes: UK release: 21 March 1983; official chronology gives 2 April for the US. The band did not tour this album.

events.title: Waters leaves; the name is disputed
events.summary: Roger Waters leaves Pink Floyd, while David Gilmour and Nick Mason decide to continue. The disagreement over the band’s future leads to a dispute about the use of its name. A later agreement permits Pink Floyd to continue with Gilmour and Mason, while Waters pursues his separate work and performances.
notes: Year precision is intentional: the official retrospective dates the announcement to October, while other accounts use December. The later settlement is described without an unsupported precise signing date.

events.title: A Momentary Lapse of Reason
events.summary: Gilmour and Mason bring Pink Floyd back to record-making with A Momentary Lapse of Reason, produced by Gilmour and Bob Ezrin. The collection moves away from a single overarching narrative toward songs with different subjects. Its release opens a new chapter for the band after Waters’ departure and the uncertainty that followed.
notes: UK release: 7 September 1987. Official chronology gives 8 September for the US.

events.summary: The new world tour opens in Ottawa, following rehearsals in Toronto. Richard Wright returns to the live band alongside Gilmour and Mason, with an expanded supporting ensemble. The concerts place the new album beside earlier Pink Floyd music, establishing continuity through performance while the group is rebuilding its recording identity.

events.summary: Delicate Sound of Thunder documents the revived touring band, drawing on performances at Nassau Coliseum in New York. events.summary: Pink Floyd performs from a floating stage in Venice, with the city itself becoming the setting for a broadcast concert. The ninety-minute show reaches television audiences in more than twenty countries. It extends the band’s concern with place and spectacle into a large public event beyond a conventional arena stage.

events.title: The Division Bell
events.summary: The Division Bell grows from renewed studio work by Gilmour, Mason and Wright, with Wright again playing a substantial creative role. Communication runs through the songs, and Polly Samson contributes lyrics. The album presents a more collective later-period sound and supplies the material for another large international tour.

events.title: Remembering Syd Barrett
events.summary: Syd Barrett dies in Cambridge. His work with Pink Floyd had been brief but foundational: the early singles and most of The Piper at the Gates of Dawn established a distinctive songwriting imagination. His death invites renewed attention to that music and to the separate life of an artist often overshadowed by his legend.
notes: The entry avoids speculation about diagnoses, causes or personal circumstances beyond the verified date and place.

events.summary: Richard Wright dies, closing the possibility of another reunion of the four musicians who performed at Live 8. Material he recorded with Gilmour and Mason during the Division Bell era later becomes the foundation of The Endless River.

events.summary: Gilmour and Mason revisit largely instrumental material recorded with Wright during the Division Bell sessions. Assisted by producers and engineers including Phil Manzanera, they shape it into The Endless River, a tribute to Wright. The mostly instrumental album closes with Louder Than Words, whose lyrics were written by Polly Samson.

Previously unreleased tracks and live documents expand the picture beyond the original albums. Its combination of audio, moving images and reproduced objects makes the early years available as a connected audiovisual history.

events.summary: Gilmour and Mason release Hey Hey Rise Up under the Pink Floyd name in support of Ukraine.
